segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for boring or bored is aburrido. Aburrido.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Aburrido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: a b u r r i d o, aburrido.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Aburrido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now this is boring or bored. One of these words in English is a characteristic, another one is a state. Which is which? Boring,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: if I say you are boring, is it a state or a characteristic?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Characteristic.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And if I say you are bored, is it a state or a characteristic?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: State.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: A state. So in English we have two different words to express this difference, whereas in Spanish you will just decide whether you're going to use ser or estar. So, you'll have to think about it. How will you say: it is boring?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es aburrido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Es aburrido. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: He is bored. Is it a characteristic or a state?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Uh, state.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So: he is bored.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Está aburrido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Está aburrido. But: he is boring.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es aburrido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And: she is boring.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es aburrido. Oh, sorry. Ella es aburrido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Mmm. Spanish is more subtle than that. (laughter) Es aburrida. Good.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es aburrida.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: They are boring.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Son aburridos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Son aburridos. They are bored.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Están aburridos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Están aburridos. So with some adjectives, we get a different meaning depending on whether we use ser or estar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for from in Spanish is de. From or of, de. De.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: De.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We get this forming part of many Latin-English words. For example, deliver, the de of deliver is actually from. Liver is to do with freedom, like liberation, liberación. How would you say: to liberate?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Liberar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Libre is free in Spanish. So again we see this grey area between v and b between English and Spanish, between libre and liver in deliver, just as we did between savvy and saber for example. So, deliver is like from or of freeing, which

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: has much more sense if you look at the original meanings of deliver, like to deliver a baby, deliver me from evil, rather than to deliver a package, which is a much more modern meaning. You can see much more the the ideology in the vocabulary with the older uses.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Another interesting word that we can see this de in in English is decipher, for example. Decipher is actually a combination of Arabic and Latin. You have de meaning of or from, and cipher from ṣifr which means zero in Arabic. So to decipher is to to go from zero, or something like this.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So anyway, we have de for from or of.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now if I want to ask: where is he from? Is it a characteristic or a state where you are from?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: A characteristic.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, it's not where you are, it's where you are from. This is characteristic of you. So in Spanish we're going to say from where are you, from where is he, from where is she, this is the word order. So, from where is what?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿De dónde?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿De dónde? From where is he, from where are you (formal), etc.?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿De dónde es?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿De dónde es? And you informal, you remember how is you are, you informal? It's kind of similar to es.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿De dónde eres?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿De dónde eres? So this sentence actually will help you remember this kind of irregular form, eres, because you will hear it all the time. ¿De dónde eres? From where are you? Where are you from?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say: where are they from?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿De dónde son?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿De dónde son? But if you want to ask: where are they? Their location. Where are they, how would you ask?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Dónde están?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Dónde están? Because now we refer to a state. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we have this adjective as well: libre, like in deliver, liberation. Libre, which means free. Again, we might mean a state or we might mean characteristic.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, sometimes to show the difference we might not just use ser and estar, we might actually also change the way we say it. So for example, if you want to say I am free, and you mean from your exams, from work, do you think you mean a state or a characteristic?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: State.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: A state. So how would you say that: I am free?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy libre.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estoy libre. And libre does not change for masculine and feminine because it ends e. Only adjectives ending o would change. Estoy libre. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now if you mean as a characteristic, as a characteristic of your personality, you are a free person, then you might say:

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Soy libre.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Soy libre. You might also say: I am a free person. So, person is persona.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And you could say, I am a What's a person?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Una persona.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I am a free person.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Soy una persona libre.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Soy una persona libre. Persona is feminine, not because of you, because the word is feminine. So I, as a male, would also say: soy una persona libre. So it's the noun in itself, persona, that is feminine.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So in this case with libre there's no problem to move between ser and estar. You can use libre with ser or with estar to give slightly different meanings. So some adjectives you will be able to move between ser and estar and others you won't. If you want to get around that uncertainty, instead of trying out soy libre you could just say soy una persona libre, and then because

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: persona is going with soy, because what you are saying in fact is I am a person, soy una persona, then you know you're safe.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Also different Spanish dialects can have different ideas about what should go with ser and what should go with estar. So for example, casado, which means married, not cansado, casado, comes from casa, literally means housed. When you are married, you are housed. (laughter) Casado, in some places they use with ser and some places they use with estar. They can't agree

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: on whether being married is a characteristic or a state. (laughter) If you want to avoid this insecurity about it, you can say: soy una persona casada. And then you know that persona is going with soy, so whatever then describes persona is not important. Persona goes with soy. When you say I am a person, then that is characteristic.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Let's explore this idea a little more. Busy in Spanish is occupied: ocupado, ocupado.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ocupado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say: I am busy?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy ocupada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estoy ocupada, or I would say estoy ocupado. Now if I want to say I'm a busy person, then with this adjective, actually I can't switch to soy and say soy ocupado, that's bad Spanish. But you as a Spanish learner, how are you supposed to know that?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you can use persona as a safety net in the sense of I am a busy person, and then you're sure it's perfect Spanish. So how would you say: I am a busy person?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Soy una persona ocupada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Soy una persona ocupada. So that's a characteristic, because what you're actually saying is I am a person, and much more characteristic than that you can't get. So estoy ocupado as a state, and then soy una persona ocupada characteristic. Males or females would say persona ocupada. Ocupada refers to persona, not to the speaker. Uh, so I would also say soy una persona ocupada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say: we are busy?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estamos ocupados.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estamos ocupados. But if you wanted to say: we are busy people?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Somos personas ocupadas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Somos personas ocupadas. To be worried is to be preoccupied. So how do you think that would sound?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Preocupado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Preocupado. I'm worried.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy preocupada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. He is worried.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Está preocupado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. He is a worried person. He is worried as a characteristic. He's worryful.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es una persona preocupada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Es una persona preocupada.
